notes: Extradition judicial review; Pitchford J dismissed challenge to Secretary of State's surrender decision after detailed delay analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Carlyle-Clarke v SSHD: extradition delay and oppression under Schedule 1
key_facts: Giles Carlyle-Clarke, a British national, was committed in January 1999 for extradition to the United States on four drug-related charges arising from alleged cannabis importation between 1986 and 1988.
The Secretary of State refused surrender in July 2002 and again in November 2003, applying the section 12(2) injustice and oppression test by practice though not by express statutory application.
The claimant argued inordinate delay by US authorities, bad faith, and that wedding photographs and other evidence showed the prosecution could have pursued him earlier.
He had been on bail since committal, acquired family responsibilities including children in Indonesia, and contended return after sixteen years would be unjust and oppressive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's second adverse extradition decision under Schedule 1 of the Extradition Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the court held the Secretary of State did not misdirect himself and his decision that return was not unjust or oppressive was within his discretion.
enrichment.ratio: On a Schedule 1 extradition reference the court reviews whether the Secretary of State lawfully applied the injustice and oppression test; unexplained delay by the requesting state is relevant but pragmatic prioritisation in a complex multi-defendant investigation does not necessarily make return oppressive, and limited non-disclosure of diplomatic correspondence does not presumptively assist the fugitive.
legal_issues: Whether delay between the alleged offences and committal rendered return unjust or oppressive
Whether the United States acted in bad faith or with culpable delay
Whether the Secretary of State was unduly credulous in accepting US explanations
Whether the court should require full disclosure of correspondence with the requesting state

notes: Unusual s.151 Companies Act appeal by controlling director seeking to void lease; Court of Appeal upheld Hart J.

enrichment.short_title: Dyment v Bishops: section 151 financial assistance and care-home lease
key_facts: Audrey Dyment, Evan Bishop and Paul Bishop operated a residential care business at The Mount through Pathways Residential and Training Centres Ltd, with the Bishops holding two-thirds of the shares.

After Council de-registration threats, the Bishops transferred their shares to Mrs Dyment in November 1991 in exchange for her interest in The Mount and a 21-year lease to the company at £66,000 per annum, well above the agreed open market rent of £37,000.

The company entered creditors' voluntary liquidation in January 1996 owing substantial rent; Mrs Dyment later admitted misfeasance and sought to expunge the Bishops' proofs by alleging unlawful financial assistance under section 151.
She was herself a director and controlling mind of the company at the time of the alleged contravention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Hart J's dismissal of an originating application in the company's liquidation challenging proofs of debt on section 151 grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; neither section 151(1) nor section 151(2) was infringed and the lease obligations remained enforceable.
enrichment.ratio: Section 151 is not contravened where the company had not become bound by the lease at the time of share acquisition and, under section 151(2), procuring the company's entry into an excessive-rent lease was for the purpose of obtaining premises to continue the business rather than for the purpose of acquiring the shares, even though share transfer was a precondition of the overall arrangement.
legal_issues: Whether escrow delivery of a lease caused the company to be bound before the tenant executed the counterpart
Whether Mrs Dyment's obligation to procure the lease was incurred for the purpose of acquiring shares
Whether the company's entry into the lease gave financial assistance to reduce that liability
Whether relation back of an escrowed lease can trigger penal section 151 consequences before the company commits itself

notes: SENDIST statutory appeal on adequacy of reasons; Wilkie J dismissed challenge to Oak Lodge placement.

enrichment.short_title: W v Harrow: SENDIST appeal on special school placement and therapy
key_facts: Mr and Mrs W's 16-year-old son with Down's syndrome, delayed speech and hearing loss had attended Parayhouse School and appealed against an amended statement naming Oak Lodge School rather than their preferred St Mary's School.
Part 3 of the statement, as amended, required on-site speech and language therapists, paediatric occupational therapists and a sizeable peer group of pupils with moderate learning difficulties.
Expert evidence from Mrs Shaffer and Parayhouse head Mrs Jackson favoured integrated on-site therapy and raised concerns about peer verbal ability and curriculum at Oak Lodge.
The Tribunal concluded Oak Lodge could deliver the agreed Part 3 provision and that attendance at the more expensive St Mary's would be an unreasonable use of public expenditure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under education legislation against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision on school placement in Part 4 of a statement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Tribunal's reasons were adequate and its preference for the local authority's therapy model over the claimants' expert evidence was not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: A SENDIST decision need only deal in summary form with substantial issues so parties know why they won or lost; where expert evidence is rejected the Tribunal should say so, but it is sufficient if the decision as a whole shows which case was preferred, and the Tribunal need not address matters outside the agreed Part 3 specification such as Italian language or sporting facilities.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal gave adequate reasons for rejecting expert evidence on on-site therapy
Whether 'on-site' therapy required therapists to be school staff rather than visiting professionals
Whether the Tribunal misunderstood evidence on peer groups and integrated communication programmes
Whether the Tribunal erred in limiting its task to matching Oak Lodge against agreed Part 3 provision

notes: Landmark inquest challenge; Collins J quashed unlawful killing verdict against police officers restraining Roger Sylvester.

enrichment.short_title: Anderson v Coroner: quashing unlawful killing verdict after s.136 restraint
key_facts: Roger Sylvester, a 30-year-old man with bipolar disorder, was detained under section 136 in January 1999 after cannabis-induced delirium and taken naked to St Ann's Hospital.
Eight police officers restrained him in the section 136 room for about fifteen to twenty minutes until he suffered cardiac arrest and died on 18 January 1999 after irreversible brain damage.
Following a delayed inquest the jury returned a verdict of unlawful killing by manslaughter-style dangerous act, citing excessive restraint duration and failure to alter position.
Six officers who participated in hospital restraint challenged the inquest on Galbraith, summing-up and perversity grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by police officers of an inquest inquisition recording unlawful killing following restraint of a section 136 patient.
enrichment.outcome: Inquisition quashed on grounds of inadequate summing-up and perverse jury reasoning; no fresh inquest ordered because no further evidence was available and a criminal conviction was unlikely.
enrichment.ratio: A verdict of unlawful killing at an inquest requires proof to the criminal standard with clear directions identifying the acts that must be found; general directions on excessive force or duration are misleading where the only viable basis was deliberate prone restraint, and a jury focus on delay awaiting medical assessment rather than restraint method shows the verdict cannot stand.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful killing should have been left to the jury under the Galbraith test
Whether the coroner adequately directed the jury on prone restraint and causation
Whether the jury's amended inquisition demonstrated misunderstanding of the law
Whether positional asphyxia guidance made prolonged prone restraint the only unlawful act in issue

notes: Permission refused on section 4B British nationality registration challenge; prior passport refusal could not retrospectively cure dual citizenship.

enrichment.short_title: Shah v SSHD: section 4B British citizenship and Indian dual nationality
key_facts: Mr Nirmal Shah, a British Overseas citizen, was wrongly refused a BOC passport in December 2001 on the ground that he was not a BOC.

The Home Office later accepted his BOC status but refused registration as a British citizen under section 4B because he remained an Indian citizen and had not lost that citizenship before 4 July 2002.
Shah argued the 2001 error should be remedied retrospectively so that grant of a BOC passport would have caused automatic loss of Indian citizenship under Indian law before the statutory cut-off.
He had not applied for section 4B registration and challenges to the 2001 and 2003 decisions were out of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review of Home Office decisions refusing British citizenship registration under section 4B.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the Secretary of State was bound to apply section 4B(2)(c) and could not waive the requirement that the applicant hold no other citizenship and not have renounced foreign nationality after 4 July 2002.
enrichment.ratio: Section 4B grants no discretion to treat an applicant as having lost foreign citizenship because of an earlier unlawful passport refusal; a passport granted on reconsideration would date from that decision without retrospective effect, and perceived injustice cannot rewrite mandatory statutory conditions.
legal_issues: Whether an erroneous 2001 BOC passport refusal could retrospectively satisfy section 4B(2)(c)
Whether the court should entertain out-of-time challenges to earlier nationality decisions
Whether Indian law automatic loss of citizenship on passport grant could be treated as having occurred in 2001
Whether Articles 6 and 8 ECHR were engaged in nationality determination
linked_authorities: Shala v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 233

confidence.notes: Short but complete judgment with clear statutory analysis and refusal of permission.

notes: Ozdemir principles applied; extension of time to appeal IAT decision refused for inadequate explanation of delay.

enrichment.short_title: Tepe v SSHD: extension of time to appeal IAT asylum decision
key_facts: Tepe, a Turkish Kurd, had his asylum appeal dismissed by the Immigration Appeal Tribunal in a decision notified on 24 July 2003 after a hearing in September 2002.
An application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal was lodged 17 days late on 26 August 2003, relying on solicitor delay and failure to apply Hayser guidelines on Kurdish asylum claims.
The IAT clerk initially had no record of the application; by April 2004 the Vice-President confirmed the Tribunal had no power to extend the ten-day limit.
The Court of Appeal notice was filed in June 2004 following informal advice from the Civil Appeals Office.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal out of time against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court refused an exceptional extension of time because delay was unexplained, not promptly pursued, and unlike Ozdemir lacked detailed supporting evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where immigration rules impose a strict ten-day limit on applications to the IAT for permission to appeal, which the IAT cannot extend, the Court of Appeal's power under CPR 52 to extend time is exceptional and requires a decision of the IAT refusing permission; unexplained solicitor delay and failure to chase a missing application will not justify extension even where the merits might have been arguable after Hayser.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction to extend time after an out-of-time IAT permission application
Whether a clerk's letter confirming refusal for want of jurisdiction constitutes a qualifying IAT decision under Ozdemir
Whether solicitor delay and loss of papers justified extension under CPR 3.9
Whether failure to apply Hayser made the underlying appeal sufficiently strong to grant relief
linked_authorities: Ozdemir v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 167

confidence.notes: Clear procedural ruling with full chronology and application of Ozdemir principles.

notes: Section 288 planning appeal dismissed; Sullivan J rejected mitigation and temporary caravan need arguments.

enrichment.short_title: Jackson v FSS: section 288 appeal against refusal of temporary caravan
key_facts: The claimant sought planning permission for a 30-foot by 10-foot cream and light green caravan for temporary residential use at Sutton Springs Trout Farm pending construction of a fishery worker's dwelling.
Winchester City Council refused permission because the caravan would be visually intrusive in an Area of Special Landscape Quality beside the River Dever.
A previous inspector had accepted functional and financial need for a dwelling but rejected the proposed permanent site on visual grounds and identified a less harmful alternative site.
The current inspector dismissed the caravan appeal, giving limited weight to the temporary nature because permission for the permanent dwelling remained uncertain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal dealt with by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the inspector lawfully rejected feather-edge screening mitigation, correctly understood the temporary need argument, and was entitled to refuse the proposed site on landscape harm grounds.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 288 appeal the court reviews the inspector's reasoning on the case as presented; a peripheral mock suggestion about feather-edge cladding was not a principal issue requiring specific consideration, and misunderstanding alleged as to immediate versus construction-phase need would not have favoured the appellant because longer occupation would increase harm.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to consider proposed feather-edge board screening mitigation
Whether the inspector mischaracterised the caravan as needed only during construction rather than until a dwelling was built
Whether the inspector adequately considered the claimant's analysis of alternative sites
Whether visual harm in an Area of Special Landscape Quality justified refusal of temporary permission

notes: Case management appeal on preliminary issue of restrictive covenant validity; limited success on third Perry affidavit only.

enrichment.short_title: LTE v Thomas: case management of preliminary restrictive covenant issue
key_facts: David Thomas sold ACE autoclave business goodwill to LTE for £600,000 and became technical director under a service agreement containing a twelve-month post-termination non-compete in clause 17.2.1.

LTE alleged Thomas breached the covenant by working for competitors Astell Scientific and ESTS after resigning on 31 March 2004 and obtained a without-notice injunction from McCombe J in September 2004.
Simon J ordered a preliminary issue on enforceability of clause 17.2.1 with written evidence only and a half-day estimate.
LTE sought at a case management conference to add expert evidence, cross-examination and a third Perry affidavit; the deputy judge largely refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal with permission granted in part against case management directions for a preliminary issue trial on restrictive covenant enforceability.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on expert evidence and cross-examination; appeal allowed only to admit paragraphs 11 onwards of Mr Perry's third affidavit with reply evidence by the respondent.
enrichment.ratio: Appellate courts should rarely interfere with case management decisions; proposed expert evidence on standard sale-of-business covenants was inadmissible or unhelpful and would jeopardise a imminent trial date, but admitting limited reply factual evidence on market and expertise caused no real prejudice where cross-examination remained for the trial judge to control.
legal_issues: Whether expert evidence on business-sale restrictive covenants should be admitted on a preliminary issue
Whether cross-examination should be ordered in advance of the preliminary issue hearing
Whether LTE should be permitted a third affidavit of Colin Perry on covenant validity
Whether negotiation-intention evidence is admissible on contractual interpretation of clause 17.2.1

notes: Major paroxetine patent appeal; Court of Appeal reversed invalidity finding and upheld non-infringement on displacing-agent construction.

enrichment.short_title: SKB v Apotex: paroxetine anhydrate patent validity and displacing agent
key_facts: SmithKline Beecham's patent 2,297,550, as amended after BASF litigation, claimed processes for making paroxetine hydrochloride anhydrate substantially free of bound organic solvent, especially isopropyl alcohol.
Apotex challenged validity over UK application 85-26407 and a 1958 erythromycin patent and denied infringement of its acetone slurry and drying process.
Pumfrey J held the patent invalid and not infringed; the main validity attack turned on whether example 1 of the 407 prior art disclosed or made obvious a water displacement step.
SKB's Seroxat product uses the hemihydrate form; the anhydrate process patent concerned solvent removal from solvate crystals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Pumfrey J's judgment holding patent 2,297,550 invalid and not infringed by Apotex's paroxetine manufacturing process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on validity; claims 1 and 2 were not anticipated or obvious over 407 or the erythromycin patent, but Apotex did not infringe because acetone was not a displacing agent within the patent's meaning.
enrichment.ratio: A displacing agent must remove bound solvent during a slurry contact step as taught by the specification, not merely during subsequent drying after acetone treatment; example 1 of 407 does not clearly disclose displacement and obviousness over it fails where Apotex's repetition experiments added unexplained nitrogen and other departures from the recipe.
legal_issues: Whether example 1 of UK application 407 anticipated or made obvious the claimed displacement process
Whether the erythromycin patent solvent displacement teaching could be combined with Buxton and Lynch
Construction of 'displacing agent' and whether Apotex's acetone process falls within the claims
Whether 'conventional drying techniques' and 'solvate' were sufficiently defined to support valid claims
